Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

input.short_description: How to declare and validate event payload shapes in Godzilla: JSON Schema, schema registries, and payload validation rules.
input.body:
Schemas

A schema is a formal declaration of the structure, types, and constraints on an event's payload. Schemas enable validation at ingestion and transformation boundaries, catch malformed data early, and provide explicit contracts between source systems and pipelines.

Why schemas matter

Without a schema, pipelines treat every incoming event as opaque JSON. This works when data is homogeneous and trusted, but quickly becomes fragile:

  • Silent failures: A missing or malformed field goes unnoticed until a transform or destination write fails downstream.
  • Type mismatches: A field that shifts from string to integer silently breaks type-aware transforms.
  • Undocumented contracts: New team members or external systems have no way to know what shape a pipeline expects.

A schema flips the burden: validation happens at the source, errors surface immediately, and the pipeline's data contract is explicit and machine-readable.

Schema formats

Godzilla supports declaring schemas in JSON Schema — the standard dialect for describing JSON structure. A typical schema looks like this:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order_schema.json|language=json|code={\n \"$schema\": \"http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#\",\n \"type\": \"object\",\n \"properties\": {\n \"order_id\": { \"type\": \"string\" },\n \"amount_cents\": { \"type\": \"integer\", \"minimum\": 0 },\n \"customer_email\": { \"type\": \"string\", \"format\": \"email\" },\n \"created_at\": { \"type\": \"string\", \"format\": \"date-time\" }\n },\n \"required\": [\"order_id\", \"amount_cents\", \"customer_email\"],\n \"additionalProperties\": false\n}}}

This schema declares that an order event must include order_id, amount_cents, and customer_email as required fields; bans any unexpected properties; and enforces type and format constraints.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=JSON Schema dialects|body_html=Godzilla currently supports JSON Schema draft 7. Other dialects (draft 4, 2019-09, 2020-12) may be supported in future releases.}}

Registering and attaching schemas

Schemas live in a schema registry — a central repository associated with your Godzilla workspace. You register a schema once, give it a name and version, and then reference it by name in any pipeline.

When a schema is attached to a pipeline's input (the source connector's output) or to a transform step, Godzilla automatically validates each incoming event against that schema. Validation failures are logged and the event is moved to the pipeline's dead-letter queue, not silently dropped.

Validation at transform boundaries

Schemas can also be attached to transform outputs. If a transform is supposed to normalize events to a known shape, attach an output schema to that step:

  • The transform's output is validated against the schema.
  • Validation failures prevent malformed events from reaching the destination.
  • Downstream transforms see a guaranteed contract.

This is especially useful in multi-stage pipelines where one transform's output feeds into another.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Schema versioning|body_html=When you update a registered schema, Godzilla treats it as a new version. Pipelines continue using the old version until you explicitly update their schema references. This prevents surprise validation failures from mid-flight schema changes.}}

Payload validation in practice

When validation is enabled on a pipeline input:

  1. An incoming event arrives from the source connector.
  2. Godzilla validates the event's payload against the attached schema.
  3. If valid, the event proceeds to transforms.
  4. If invalid, the validation error is recorded and the event moves to the dead-letter queue.

The validation report includes the specific constraint that failed (e.g., "missing required field customer_email" or "amount_cents must be ≥ 0"), making debugging straightforward.

Relationship to Events

Every event has a payload; a schema is the optional but recommended way to declare what that payload must look like. Schemas are not required — Godzilla is happy to process unvalidated JSON events — but they catch errors early and make your pipelines more robust.

input.body:
Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={\n \"id\": \"evt_8f2c1a90\",\n \"type\": \"order.created\",\n \"occurred_at\": \"2026-08-18T09:12:44Z\",\n \"source\": \"connector_postgres_orders\",\n \"payload\": { \"order_id\": \"ord_4471\", \"amount_cents\": 4899 }\n}}}

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Validating event payloads with schemas

By default, pipelines accept events with any JSON payload. To enforce a structure, attach a schema to your pipeline's input or to individual transform steps. Schemas validate payloads against JSON Schema constraints and move invalid events to the dead-letter queue, catching data quality issues early.

See Schemas to learn how to declare and register schemas for your events.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

input.body:
{{ds:component/hero|title=Concepts|subtitle=The three building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.|cta_html=Start with Pipelines}}

Godzilla is built from three ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/5ac66235-69dc-4092-b430-9d68837e0c76}}|tag=Concept|title=Pipelines|description=Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/7418c3d6-9ea1-4d1c-8d8f-73136f6b6abb}}|tag=Concept|title=Connectors|description=Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/6277e4fb-3e99-45b0-a7f6-aefe69c5778f}}|tag=Concept|title=Events|description=The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.}}

Declaring and validating event structures

Once you understand pipelines, connectors, and events, the next step is learning how to formally declare what your event payloads look like and validate them in flight.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/f2e5fa8f-30dc-4d9b-8c88-15cc24fadec4}}|tag=Concept|title=Schemas|description=JSON Schema declarations and validation rules to ensure event payload integrity across your pipelines.}}

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.

To ensure data quality, you can attach schemas to validate event payloads at the pipeline input or at transform boundaries.
